stories.headline: Update: Trump Says Pardon for Nvidia's Huang 'Always an Option' as Financial Disclosures Show Trump Holds Millions in Nvidia Stock
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump told the New York Post on Tuesday that pardoning reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is "always an option, I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary." Huang returned to the company after its board unanimously reinstated him, following input from the U.S. government indicating his return poses no national security risk. Huang is scheduled to testify before congressional committees, including a Senate hearing on Dec. 3, and Trump urged him to "tell the truth."

New details emerged on Wednesday about Trump's financial stake. Disclosure documents reviewed by ABC News show the president owned at least $12 million in Nvidia stock at the end of 2025, and other reports put his holdings in the tens of millions. Attorney General Todd Blanche called Nvidia "a good corporate citizen" while declining to detail the Justice Department's role. U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly told congressional aides there was no evidence that a woman at the center of the scandal took direction from Chinese intelligence. Huang acknowledged he had violated the company's code of conduct and "made some terrible mistakes."

The reaction on Capitol Hill has been bipartisan. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer accused Huang of shipping advanced chips to China in violation of export controls and has vowed an investigation, while lawmakers in both parties are pushing chip export restrictions in the year-end defense bill. Supporters of the administration have framed the move as protecting a key American technology champion, while critics, including some Republicans, say it shows different rules for the powerful. Nvidia shares have swung sharply since the reinstatement, with tech stocks dipping amid the controversy.

stories.headline: Medvedev Says Russia Could Launch 'Preventive Nuclear Attack' Over Ukraine
stories.summary:
Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev, now deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, warned Monday that Moscow could carry out a "preventive nuclear attack" under certain circumstances. In an article in the Moscow Journal of International Law, excerpted by the state news agency TASS, he wrote that "the massive use of non-nuclear means that cause catastrophes makes a preventive nuclear attack by the Russian Federation possible."

Medvedev also said "secret or hidden supplies of nuclear weapons from the West to Kyiv will provoke a legitimate preventive nuclear attack by Russia." He argued that Ukraine, NATO members and several Western countries outside the alliance have already created situations in which Russia could consider a nuclear strike, and that Russia has "not only the right, but in various situations the obligation" to use such weapons.

He tempered the language by saying President Vladimir Putin weighs the proportionality of any response and that events so far have not created a "direct necessity" for nuclear use. The warning comes nearly five years into the war and amid tension between Moscow and the West over NATO support for Kyiv, and shortly after Trump, Putin and Xi held talks in China that touched on nuclear arms. Medvedev has a record of inflammatory nuclear rhetoric, and Western officials have often treated such statements as signaling rather than policy.

stories.headline: Fed's Preferred Inflation Gauge Rises to 3.8% in October Ahead of December Meeting
stories.summary:
The Bureau of Economic Analysis reported Wednesday that the personal consumption expenditures price index rose 0.3 percent in October and was up 3.8 percent from a year earlier. That is a two-tenths of a point increase from the prior annual reading and the highest since May, driven largely by soaring energy prices.

The PCE index is the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation measure, and inflation has now been above the central bank's 2 percent target for five years and eight months. The report is the last major inflation reading before the Fed's final rate-setting meeting of 2026, scheduled in about two weeks.

The Hill reported that the Fed is widely expected to raise interest rates at the meeting. Persistent inflation has weighed on consumer confidence and added to pressure on households during the Thanksgiving period, when food costs are also higher. The decision will be closely watched by markets, which have been volatile amid the AI-sector selloff and trade tensions.

stories.headline: Solomon Islands Ends Security Pact With China, Signs Treaty With Australia
stories.summary:
The Solomon Islands signed a "historic" treaty with Australia on Wednesday, after reportedly telling China it would not renew a 2022 security pact. At a press conference in Canberra, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and his Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale said the treaty would make Australia the Pacific nation's "security partner of choice."

The 2022 pact with Beijing, signed under then-leader Manasseh Sogavare, was never publicly released, but leaked excerpts showed it allowed Chinese police deployments and a possible quasi-military base. It prompted alarm in Washington and Canberra. Australian media reported Tuesday that Honiara had told Beijing it would not renew the deal, understood to expire in April 2027. Wale said there were "ongoing discussions" with China but he could not discuss the pact due to a non-disclosure agreement. China's foreign ministry neither confirmed nor denied the termination, saying cooperation with Pacific nations involves no "geopolitical rivalry."

Under the treaty, the Solomon Islands commits to consult Australia on critical infrastructure and to limit security cooperation to Pacific Islands Forum members. Analysts called it an enormous win for Canberra that closes the loop on security deals Australia struck with Pacific nations after the China pact. Wale said the new treaty marks a reset: "Those days are done, gone."

stories.headline: Update: Democrats Expand House Majority to 259 Seats With Tennessee Upset
stories.summary:
Democrat Victoria Broderick, 34, won Tennessee's 4th congressional district, unseating eight-term Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais. The seat was carried by Donald Trump by more than 20 points in 2024, making it one of the biggest House upsets of the cycle. Her victory lifts Democrats to at least 259 seats in the 120th Congress, the party's largest House majority in three decades.

The result adds to a broad Democratic showing in the November midterms. Democrats have also clinched the Senate and flipped at least 12 state legislative chambers, according to coverage in the pool. Hakeem Jeffries is expected to become the next speaker of the House.

Republicans are now debating who should bear responsibility for the losses. Reports describe President Trump's handpicked party chair fending off a challenge from a colleague, while some House Republicans are urging Secretary of State Marco Rubio to consider a 2028 presidential run as a party unifier. Democrats, for their part, are weighing leadership questions of their own, including calls from some in the party for a change at the top of the Senate caucus, and are beginning to size up a wide-open 2028 presidential field.

The new majority will take office as Congress faces a stopgap spending bill and fights over an energy permitting overhaul, both of which will shape the early agenda. Republican supporters of the president point to the historically difficult midterm environment for the party in power, while Democrats describe the results as a rebuke of Trump's second-term agenda.

stories.headline: Merz Warns Russia's War Aims Extend Beyond Ukraine, Pledges Continued Aid
stories.summary:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Moscow's ambitions reach well beyond Ukraine and pledged that Germany will maintain its military support for Kyiv. His remarks come as the war spreads into new theaters and as NATO members voice growing unease about the conflict's geographic expansion.

Ukraine has recently attacked Russian-linked ships in distant waters, including strikes at a Libyan port that Kyiv says sank Russian vessels. Libya's eastern commander Khalifa Haftar, whose forces Russia backs, vowed retaliation for the deaths of his soldiers. He is now making a rare visit to Turkey, a trip that risks complicating Ankara's efforts to reunify the divided North African nation.

Separately, Poland said it has renewed its push for a permanent US military presence after two Russian airspace incursions in four days. In one, a Swedish fighter jet operating under NATO command was cleared to shoot down a Russian cruise missile but held its fire.

Merz's message is aimed at reinforcing European resolve at a time when allies are weighing the cost of sustained support. Critics of continued aid in some European capitals argue for negotiation, while Berlin and its closest partners contend that a Russian success in Ukraine would embolden further aggression against NATO states.

stories.headline: Update: Colombian Forces Storm Cartagena Supermarket, Free 20 Hostages After 17 Hours
stories.summary:
Colombian special forces and police stormed a supermarket in a Cartagena shopping mall and freed about 20 shoppers and employees held hostage for roughly 17 hours. One gunman was killed and four were arrested. Police said they used stun grenades to overpower the hostage takers, and nearby residents reported hearing explosions.

The gunmen entered the building at 8 a.m. Tuesday after a failed attempt to rob an armored car carrying cash. They demanded safe passage, armored vehicles and nearly $2 million. They released 10 hostages earlier in the day, including elderly women, but kept around 20 as a police helicopter hovered overhead.

President Abelardo de la Espriella flew to Cartagena to oversee the operation and authorized the assault, calling it an extraordinary joint operation carried out flawlessly. He said the gunmen had no political affiliations and were criminals caught off guard who then took hostages. Authorities reportedly feared some attackers might try to pass themselves off as hostages during the rescue.

The freed hostages were examined by medical teams and reunited with relatives who had waited for hours outside the security perimeter. The identities of the four arrested suspects have not been released.

stories.headline: South African Court Sets Aside Report Behind Ramaphosa Impeachment Threat
stories.summary:
The Western Cape High Court ruled that a parliamentary panel report finding President Cyril Ramaphosa may have a case to answer over the Phala Phala farm theft was unlawful, setting it aside in its entirety. Judge Nolwazi Mabindla-Boqwana said the panel misconstrued its function and made several material errors of law. The court also declared unlawful the steps parliament took in relation to the report.

The 2022 report concerned the theft of about $580,000 hidden in a sofa at Ramaphosa's Limpopo game farm in 2020. It cited substantial doubt about the legitimacy of the cash's source. Ramaphosa has denied wrongdoing, saying the money came from a legitimate sale of buffalo, and several earlier investigations cleared him.

The ruling effectively removes the basis for impeachment proceedings. Those had been revived after the Constitutional Court found in May that parliament acted unconstitutionally by blocking an impeachment inquiry. Earlier this month, two people were found guilty of the theft itself.

Opposition parties have said they intend to challenge the decision, so the matter is likely to return to the courts. The outcome is significant for the stability of Ramaphosa's government.
